slides.title: Chapter 3: Bitcoin Core
slides.notes: Chapter 2 followed one payment through the network. Chapter 3 opens the program that checks every rule, Bitcoin Core, and shows how to build it, run it and ask it questions. Every result in this deck was computed by the chapter library from saved data.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.take: Seven parts, three true stories, nineteen examples
slides.notes: The route has seven parts that follow the program from its source code to the toolkits around it. Three true stories and nineteen code examples are spread across them. Every example has a picture of its result.

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers

items: What makes Bitcoin Core the reference implementation of Bitcoin?
How do I choose a release, check it and build it from source?
Which settings decide what a node stores, remembers and trusts?
How do I ask a running node questions, and who may ask?
How do I decode a transaction and tell its txid from its weight?
How can I check a block myself, and what else can talk to a node?

slides.notes: The six questions are the chapter's own, rewritten so that each has an answer on a slide. We return to them in the summary. A reader who can answer all six has understood the chapter.

slides.title: The chapter in one picture
slides.take: Six steps from the source code to the data of the chain
slides.notes: Six steps carry us from the source code to the data of the chain. We read the code and pick a release, build it, run it, ask it questions and read what it says. The last step looks at other programs that speak to a node.

slides.title: From Bitcoin to Bitcoin Core
slides.sub: Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation

items.meaning: The program against which other programs are measured.
items.analogy: Think of the standard metre bar that every ruler was checked against.

items.meaning: A node that downloads every block and checks every rule itself.
items.analogy: Think of an auditor who recounts every receipt instead of trusting a summary.

items.meaning: A numbered public document that proposes a change to Bitcoin.
items.analogy: Think of a numbered bylaw proposed in a club's rulebook.

slides.notes: Part 1 asks what Bitcoin Core is. It began as the program Satoshi Nakamoto released in 2009, and it checks every rule itself as a full verification node. Changes reach it through numbered Bitcoin Improvement Proposals.

slides.title: Version 0.1, set in stone
slides.sub: 8 January 2009 · the first release of Bitcoin

items.cap: Picture: Satoshi bust, Budapest - Fekist, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHO Satoshi Nakamoto, the pseudonymous author of the white paper and of the first program.
WHAT Version 0.1 of Bitcoin, a Windows program that anyone could download and run.
WHERE Announced on the metzdowd.com cryptography mailing list; the download sat on SourceForge.
WHY Only running software could start the network. Later he wrote that, once 0.1 was out, the core design was set in stone.
HOW A short post with the download link, five days after the first block had been mined.

items.who: Satoshi Nakamoto, announcing on the metzdowd.com cryptography mailing list

slides.take: The program came first: the reference implementation defines the rules
slides.notes: In January 2009 Satoshi Nakamoto published version 0.1 of the Bitcoin program. A year and a half later he wrote that its core design was set in stone. That is why Bitcoin Core is called the reference implementation: the software came first, and the rules are what it does.

slides.title: Inside the program
slides.take: One program: it listens, checks, stores and answers
slides.notes: Bitcoin Core is one program with several parts. Peers and the connection manager bring in blocks and transactions, the validation engine checks them, and the storage engine keeps headers, blocks and coins. The interface at the right lets your own programs ask questions.

slides.title: A version number that carries a vote
slides.sub: A Bitcoin Improvement Proposal signals through bit flags
slides.take: Think of a ballot with 29 tick boxes, one for each proposal
slides.notes: A block's version field is not a counter. Its top three bits mark the BIP 9 scheme, and every lower bit is a vote for one proposal. Here only bit 1 is set.

slides.title: Bitcoin Development Environment
slides.sub: Compiling Bitcoin Core from the Source Code

items.meaning: A name that fixes one exact version of the source, such as v31.1.
items.analogy: Think of a bookmark that always opens the same page.

items.meaning: A tagged version offered for testing before it becomes final.
items.analogy: Think of a dress rehearsal before the opening night.

items.meaning: The node program, which runs in the background.
items.analogy: Think of the engine of a car, working while you do other things.

slides.notes: Part 2 turns the source code into programs you can run. A release tag fixes which version you build, and release candidates are tried before a final tag exists. The build produces bitcoind, the node itself.

slides.title: Three steps from source to executables
slides.take: Select, configure, build: three steps, one set of programs
slides.notes: A build has three decisions. You select a release tag, you configure which features to build, and you build the executables. Each step has a single command, and a clean tag makes the result repeatable.

slides.title: Release tags sort by number, not by letters
slides.sub: A release tag names the version; a release candidate carries rc
slides.take: Think of edition numbers: the tenth edition follows the ninth
slides.notes: These are real tags of the Bitcoin repository. Sorted as text, v0.10.0 lands before v0.9.5, which is wrong. A release candidate is a tag with rc in it, so we leave those out first.

slides.title: What a release folder holds
slides.sub: bitcoind is the node; bitcoin-cli is the client that calls it
slides.take: Think of bitcoind as the engine and bitcoin-cli as the steering wheel
slides.notes: A release unpacks into seven programs and three helper parts. The one to know is bitcoind, the node. You steer it from the command line with bitcoin-cli.

slides.title: Dozens of builders, one identical binary
slides.sub: 13 September 2021 · Bitcoin Core 22.0 moves to Guix

items.cap: Picture: GNU Guix logo - GNU Guix, public domain, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHO Carl Dong, who wrote the Guix build system, and the independent builders who sign its results.
WHAT Release 22.0 was the first built with Guix, so anyone can rebuild the binary bit for bit.
WHEN 2021-09-13 (13 September 2021)
WHERE The guix.sigs repository, beside bitcoin/bitcoin on GitHub.
WHY A downloaded program asks for trust; here several builders compare hashes instead of taking one person's word.
HOW Each builder compiles the tagged source and signs the hashes. Release 31.1 shows 11 good signatures on its SHA256SUMS.

items.who: Carl Dong, who wrote the Guix build system that Bitcoin Core adopted for release 22.0, and the independent builders who sign its results

slides.take: Verify, don't trust: the project applies its own rule to itself
slides.notes: Anyone can ask whether a downloaded binary really matches the source. Since release 22.0 Bitcoin Core builds with Guix, so independent builders get identical files and sign their hashes. For release 31.1 the checksum file carries eleven good signatures.

slides.title: A download must match its published hash
slides.sub: Checking a release against SHA256SUMS
slides.take: Think of the safety seal on a medicine bottle: break it and you can tell
slides.notes: Each release ships a list of hashes. You hash your download and compare. If the two texts match, the file is the one that the builders signed for.

slides.title: Running a Bitcoin Core Node
slides.sub: Configuring the Bitcoin Core Node

items.meaning: A text file of settings that the node reads when it starts.
items.analogy: Think of the settings card taped to a coffee machine.

items.meaning: The folder in which the node keeps blocks, state, logs and settings.
items.analogy: Think of the node's filing cabinet.

items.meaning: An option that deletes old block files after the node has checked them.
items.analogy: Think of an accountant who audits old invoices, keeps the totals and shreds the paper.

slides.notes: Part 3 starts the node and sets it up. A configuration file and the command line decide what the node does, and the data directory is where it keeps everything. Pruning, the transaction index and the memory limits trade disk, memory and features.

slides.title: The command line wins over the file
slides.sub: The configuration file sets defaults; an option on the command line overrides them
slides.take: Think of a recipe card that you may override with a note on the fridge
slides.notes: A configuration file holds the settings of a node. When the same option is also given on the command line, the command line wins. A script can therefore change one value for one run.

slides.title: Inside the data directory
slides.sub: What the offline node of release 31.1 had written
slides.take: The data directory is the whole memory of the node
slides.notes: Everything the node knows lives in its data directory. Blocks and the chain state are the big parts, the log is the node's diary, and the configuration file holds your settings. The cookie file appears while the node runs.

slides.title: How the database cache is shared out
slides.sub: The dbcache setting is divided before it is used
slides.take: Think of a desk: two small drawers and one very large tabletop
slides.notes: The dbcache option sizes the cache for the unspent outputs. Bitcoin Core first gives two small databases their share. Everything else goes to the cache of coins.

slides.title: Pruning and the transaction index do not mix
slides.sub: prune deletes old blocks; txindex needs every block
slides.take: Think of a library that shreds old books and so cannot catalogue them all
slides.notes: Pruning keeps only recent blocks. The transaction index must find any block that holds a transaction. The node therefore refuses both at once, and release 31.1 printed exactly that.

slides.title: Two ways to spend less memory
slides.sub: The blocksonly and maxmempool options
slides.take: A node can trade features for memory, and keep verifying everything
slides.notes: Two settings reduce what a node asks of its machine. Blocks-only mode stops it from collecting loose transactions, and the mempool limit caps the waiting room. The default limit is 300 megabytes, and blocks-only mode needs only 5.

slides.title: An alert text is cleaned before it runs
slides.sub: The alertnotify option runs your command when the node raises an alert
slides.take: Think of a mail room that removes anything dangerous before a letter reaches you
slides.notes: The node can run a script of yours when something is wrong. The message goes into the command, so the node cleans it first. The hostile quotes vanish and the rest stays inside one word.

slides.title: The project that outlives its keyholders
slides.sub: 7 April 2014 · Andresen hands over to van der Laan

items.cap: Picture: Gavin Andresen, 2014 - Stephen McCarthy, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHO Gavin Andresen, who led the software after Satoshi Nakamoto, and Wladimir van der Laan, his successor.
WHAT Andresen passed the lead-maintainer role of Bitcoin Core to van der Laan.
WHERE The public bitcoin/bitcoin repository on GitHub, where every change is reviewed in the open.
WHY Andresen wanted to focus on protocol work, and a reference cannot wait for one person.
HOW He named van der Laan, who led until 2022; Satoshi had handed the project to Andresen in 2011.

items.who: Satoshi Nakamoto, Gavin Andresen and Wladimir van der Laan, who passed the lead role of the Bitcoin software on in 2011 and 2014
items.where: the public bitcoin/bitcoin repository on GitHub

slides.take: The reference implementation is an institution, not a person
slides.notes: Bitcoin Core outlived its first author. Satoshi Nakamoto handed the project to Gavin Andresen in 2011, and on 7 April 2014 Andresen passed the lead to Wladimir van der Laan. A reference implementation needs a team and public review, not one keyholder.

slides.title: Bitcoin Core API
slides.sub: Getting Information on Bitcoin Core's Status

items.meaning: A command-line tool that calls the node's interface.
items.analogy: Think of a remote control for the node.

items.meaning: A way to call a program's functions with small JSON messages.
items.analogy: Think of an order slip handed over a counter.

items.meaning: A secret that the node writes to a file at every start.
items.analogy: Think of a hotel key card coded anew for each guest.

items.meaning: A stored user name with a salted hash of the password.
items.analogy: Think of a bank that keeps a check value, not your PIN.

slides.notes: Part 4 talks to the running node. The command-line client bitcoin-cli sends JSON-RPC calls, and the node checks who is asking before it answers. The cookie is the default way in, and rpcauth is the fixed alternative.

slides.title: One JSON-RPC call and its reply
slides.sub: JSON-RPC is how every client talks to the node
slides.take: Think of an order slip: the same fields every time, and an answer on the same slip
slides.notes: A call is a small JSON text with a method and parameters. The reply carries a result, an error and the id of the call. The sample reply is the one the book prints for the curl example.

slides.title: The cookie is a fresh password
slides.sub: Cookie authentication needs no password to invent or store
slides.take: Think of a hotel key card that is recoded for every guest
slides.notes: At every start bitcoind writes a new random secret to the .cookie file. A client that can read the file can call the node. The secret is 32 bytes, shown as 64 hexadecimal characters.

slides.title: rpcauth stores a salted hash, not the password
slides.sub: A fixed credential for programs that cannot read the cookie
slides.take: Think of a bank that keeps a check value and never your PIN
slides.notes: The rpcauth line holds a user, a random salt and a keyed hash of the password. Even a leaked configuration file does not reveal the password. A wrong password gives a different hash.

slides.title: Reading getblockchaininfo
slides.sub: Getting Information on Bitcoin Core's Status
slides.take: Think of a car dashboard: it reports, and you do not touch the engine
slides.notes: This is the answer of a real node of release 31.1 that had only the first block. It says which chain it is on, how many blocks it has verified and how hard the work is.

slides.title: Exploring and Decoding Transactions
slides.sub: Reading a transaction the way the node reports it

items.meaning: The hash that names a transaction.
items.analogy: Think of the tracking number on a parcel.

items.meaning: Changing a transaction's id without changing what it does.
items.analogy: Think of a receipt whose number changes when the clerk re-signs it.

items.meaning: The measure by which a block is filled.
items.analogy: Think of postage by volume, where compact data costs less.

slides.notes: Part 5 reads a transaction the way the node reports it. Each transaction has an identifier, a weight and a witness. We decode Alice's payment from chapter 2 and look at each part.

slides.title: Decoding Alice's transaction
slides.sub: Exploring and Decoding Transactions
slides.take: Think of an X-ray: the same body, shown layer by layer
slides.notes: The node's own decoder turns Alice's bytes into readable fields. Every output has a number, a value and a type. Two outputs, 20,000 and 75,000 satoshis, plus the 5,000 fee make her 100,000.

slides.title: The txid leaves the witness out
slides.sub: The transaction ID and transaction malleability
slides.take: Think of a tracking number printed before anyone adds a signature
slides.notes: The txid is a hash of the transaction without its witness. A third party can no longer change the txid by re-encoding a signature. That change is called transaction malleability, and segregated witness ended it.

slides.title: Weight units and virtual bytes
slides.sub: How much of a block a transaction fills
slides.take: Think of postage by volume: compact, light data costs less
slides.notes: Blocks are filled by weight units. Base bytes count four units each and witness bytes one. Alice's 194 bytes weigh 569 units, which is 143 virtual bytes.

slides.title: Exploring Blocks
slides.sub: Height, hash, merkle root and time

items.meaning: A block's place in the chain, counted from zero.
items.analogy: Think of a page number in a very long book.

items.meaning: The name of a block, made by hashing its header.
items.analogy: Think of a fingerprint taken from the page's header.

items.meaning: The middle timestamp of the last eleven blocks.
items.analogy: Think of a median price that one odd sale cannot move.

slides.notes: Part 6 reads blocks. A block has a height, a hash made from its header, a merkle root of its transactions and a time. We rebuild each one ourselves with a few lines of Python.

slides.title: Height, depth and confirmations
slides.sub: Example numbers: block 123,456 with five blocks on top
slides.take: A confirmation is one more block on top of yours
slides.notes: A block's height counts the blocks before it, so the first block has height zero. Each block built on top adds a confirmation. The numbers in the picture are an example, not a live chain.

slides.title: A block's name is the hash of its header
slides.sub: The block hash and the block height of block 123,456
slides.take: Think of a fingerprint taken from the page's header line
slides.notes: The header has six fields in 80 bytes. Hashing it twice and reversing the bytes gives the block hash, which starts with many zeros. The block's height, 123,456, counts the blocks before it.

slides.title: Rebuilding the merkle root
slides.sub: One hash that commits to every transaction of the block
slides.take: Think of a tournament bracket: pairs play, winners meet, one champion remains
slides.notes: Block 123,456 holds 13 transactions. Hashing neighbours in pairs gives 7, 4, 2 and finally 1 hash. That last hash is the merkle root stored in the header, and one changed transaction would change it.

slides.title: Median time of the last eleven blocks
slides.sub: Block timestamps are guesses; the median time is not
slides.take: Think of a median price that one odd sale cannot move
slides.notes: Miners write the time into every header, and it can be a little off. Bitcoin Core therefore uses the median of the last eleven times. We recompute the saved median of block 123,456.

slides.title: Alternative Clients, Libraries, and Toolkits
slides.sub: Using Bitcoin Core's Programmatic Interface

items.meaning: A Python library that calls the node and builds transactions.
items.analogy: Think of a phrasebook that turns your Python into the node's language.

items.meaning: Another program that follows Bitcoin's rules.
items.analogy: Think of another airline flying the same routes under the same safety rules.

slides.notes: Part 7 looks beyond Bitcoin Core. Libraries such as python-bitcoinlib call the node from your own programs, and other clients follow the same rules in other languages. We end with how fresh each toolkit is.

slides.title: Using Bitcoin Core's Programmatic Interface
slides.sub: python-bitcoinlib calls the node for you
slides.take: Your code can ask the node anything the command line can
slides.notes: A library can speak to the node for you. python-bitcoinlib builds the JSON-RPC call, sends it over HTTP and returns the result as a Python value. On the offline node of release 31.1 a call for the block count returned zero.

slides.title: How fresh are the alternative toolkits
slides.sub: python-bitcoinlib and its neighbours, by days since the latest release
slides.take: Think of the date on the newest delivery in a shop window
slides.notes: Libraries for other languages and other clients exist, but they age. This is the number of days between each toolkit's latest release and the day we asked the registries. A library can be useful and still be old.

slides.title: Summary: the six answers
slides.take: Reference, release, settings, interface, transaction, block
slides.notes: Each row answers one of the six opening questions in a line. If you can say each answer in your own words, using the everyday pictures of this chapter, you have the chapter.
